title: Low rank adaptation of chemical foundation models generate effective odorant representations
claim: Fixed-feature and fully supervised approaches underperform; fine-tuning pretrained foundation models strikes the balance and yields better representations.
layout: 3 panels: foundation models top-left, three-way approach comparison bottom, conceptual curve top-right
description: Panel A, top left, shows two shaded boxes: a blue Chemical Foundation Model (Transformer/GNN, a column of dark dots, projection head, odorant pretext task) and a pink Protein Foundation Model with the same structure in red. Panel B, along the bottom, compares three approaches side by side: Supervised (a fully trained GNN plus a fixed protein encoder), Feature Based (both encoders fixed), and Fine-tuning Based (LORAX, with fine-tuned chemical weights). Each takes a molecule drawing and a receptor icon and feeds into an 'Affinity Prediction' box. The first two end in a red thumbs-down and the LORAX version ends in a green thumbs-up. Panel C, top right, is a conceptual inverted-U curve of odorant representation efficacy. Red, orange and blue dots mark the feature-based, fine-tuning and supervised approaches, with a dashed baseline.
caption: LORAX presents a new approach to incorporate chemical foundation models to predict odorant-receptor affinity. (A) General architecture of chemical and protein foundation models. (B) Current approaches, and our proposed approach (right), to predicting affinity of odorant-receptor binding. (C) Putative thought model given our approach and results: we hypothesize that fine-tuning allows for creation of improved odorant representations that outperform existing approaches.
abstract: Featurizing odorants to enable robust prediction of their properties is difficult due to the complex activation patterns that odorants evoke in the olfactory system. Structurally similar odorants can elicit distinct activation patterns in both the sensory periphery (i.e., at the receptor level) and downstream brain circuits (i.e., at a perceptual level). Despite efforts to design odorant features to better predict how they interact with the olfactory system, there is still no universally accepted approach to this problem. We demonstrate that feature-based approaches that rely on pre-trained foundation models to generate odorant representations $\textit{do not}$ significantly outperform classical hand-designed features on odorant-receptor binding tasks. Instead, we show that it is necessary to fine-tune these features to increase predictive performance. To show this, we introduce a new model that creates olfaction-specific representations: $\textbf{L}$oRA-based $\textbf{O}$dorant-$\textbf{R}$eceptor $\textbf{A}$ffinity prediction with $\textbf{CROSS}$-attention ($\textbf{LORAX}$). We compare existing chemical foundation model representations to hand-designed physicochemical descriptors using feature-based methods and identify large information overlap between these representations, highlighting the necessity of fine-tuning to generate novel and superior odorant representations. We show that LORAX produces a feature space more closely aligned with olfactory neural representation, enabling it to outperform existing models on predictive tasks.
